cues.text: Chapter four looks at strategic alignment and competitive advantage.
This is where we stop asking what a technology can do, and start asking what it is for.
Let us begin with strategic IT-business alignment.
Alignment means two things working together.
First, technology decisions support business goals.
Second, business strategy understands the opportunities that technology offers.
So influence flows in both directions.
The business should not simply hand over a list of demands to the technology team, and the technology team should not simply build whatever looks impressive.
How do we achieve it?
The source gives us a sequence of steps.
First, define a measurable goal.
A goal you cannot measure is a wish.
Second, map the capabilities required to reach that goal.
Third, prioritise initiatives, because an organisation never has the money or people to do everything at once.
Fourth, assign ownership and budgets, so that every initiative has a named person responsible and the resources to proceed.
Fifth, monitor benefits, so that you check whether the promised value actually arrives.
Throughout all of this, IT leaders and business leaders share accountability.
If an initiative fails, it is not only the technology team's failure, and if it succeeds, the credit is shared too.
Now let us bring in a classic lens: Porter's competitive strategies.
Michael Porter described three ways a firm can compete.
The first is cost leadership, which means achieving lower unit costs than rivals.
The second is differentiation, which means offering distinctive value that customers recognise and prefer.
The third is focus, which means choosing a particular segment and serving it especially well.
Digital tools can enable each of these.
Consider three examples from the source.
A retailer uses demand forecasting to reduce waste.
That supports cost leadership, because less stock is thrown away or left unsold, so unit costs fall.
A payment service differentiates itself through reliable, convenient transactions.
Customers choose it because it works when they need it and is easy to use.
And an education platform serves underserved learners.
That is a focus strategy, because it concentrates on a chosen segment that others may neglect.
But here is an important warning.
A tool that competitors can buy is rarely a durable advantage by itself.
If you can purchase it, so can they.
So where does lasting advantage come from?
The source lists defensible capabilities that may arise from data quality, customer trust, operational expertise, integration, network effects and continuous learning.
Notice that these are things an organisation builds over time, not things it simply installs.
Network effects, for instance, mean that a service becomes more valuable as more people use it.
Integration means technology is woven into how the whole organisation operates, rather than sitting alone as a separate system.
This leads us to the resource-based view.
This approach asks whether a resource is valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and organisationally supported.
Those four tests are abbreviated as VRIO, pronounced V-R-I-O.
Valuable: does it help the firm create worth?
Rare: do few competitors have it?
Imitation: is it hard for others to copy?
And Organisation: is the firm set up, through its processes, structure and culture, to actually exploit it?
The source gives a clear illustration.
A sophisticated recommendation engine provides little value if the data is poor or if customers do not trust it.
The engine may be technically impressive, yet it fails the test because the supporting resources are missing.
This is why strategic alignment matters: it links the investment to outcomes, rather than to novelty.
Now we turn to financial evaluation.
Start with total cost of ownership.
This includes acquisition, implementation, integration, operations, training, maintenance and exit costs.
Many people count only the purchase price, but the real cost runs across the whole life of the system, including the cost of eventually leaving it.
Then there is return on investment, or ROI.
The formula is: ROI equals benefits minus costs, divided by costs, multiplied by one hundred percent.
Let us work through the source example step by step.
Suppose a service costs twenty million naira over a period, and yields twenty-eight million naira of measurable benefits.
First, subtract costs from benefits: twenty-eight million minus twenty million is eight million naira.
Second, divide that by the costs: eight million divided by twenty million gives zero point four.
Third, multiply by one hundred percent, and we get forty percent.
So the simple ROI is forty percent.
The source adds cautions.
Do not mistake revenue for net benefit, because revenue is what comes in, not what remains after costs.
And do not ignore security and migration costs, which are easy to overlook.
Finally, establish a baseline, a benefits owner and a measurement horizon.
The baseline is the starting position you compare against.
The benefits owner is the person accountable for delivering the gains.
And the measurement horizon is the period over which you will judge the results.
Last, let us consider how we measure success.
Useful KPIs, or key performance indicators, include adoption, customer satisfaction, service availability, transaction completion rate, cycle time, cost per transaction and digital revenue.
Cycle time is how long a process takes from start to finish.
Now, a vital distinction.
An output is a deployed application.
An outcome is improved customer access, cost or revenue.
An output tells you that work was delivered; an outcome tells you that it mattered.
A team can ship an application, which is an output, and still have no change in customer access, which is the outcome.
To keep our measurement balanced, the source offers the balanced scorecard.
It considers four perspectives: financial, customer, internal process, and learning.
Together they stop an organisation from judging success by money alone, and encourage it to look at customers, at how work gets done, and at how well the organisation is learning and improving.

So, to bring the chapter together: align technology with measurable business goals, use strategy lenses to understand how to compete, build capabilities that rivals cannot easily copy, justify investment with honest financial analysis, and measure outcomes rather than just outputs.
